questions.question: Give the four arguments for why manufacturing matters more to South Africa than its GDP share suggests.
questions.expected_answer: Value added — manufacturing multiplies the worth of primary produce and keeps the difference at home (the case for beneficiation); employment quality and multipliers — formal year-round jobs each supporting supplier, transport and retail jobs; linkages — backward to the primary sector and forward to tertiary services, making it the bridge of the economy; and export diversification — manufactured exports, led by vehicles, cushion the economy against single-commodity price swings.

questions.question: Explain, using the transport-cost logic, why a sugar mill and a brewery locate at opposite ends of their supply chains.
questions.expected_answer: The factory sits at the end that is more expensive to move. Sugar cane is heavy, perishable and loses most of its weight in processing, so mills locate at the cane fields and ship the light sugar — raw-material orientation. A brewery's inputs (malt, hops) travel easily, but its output is heavy, fragile bottled liquid, and bread similarly stales — so breweries and bakeries locate at the market. Compare which end is heavier, bulkier or quicker to spoil; the plant sits at the difficult end.

questions.question: List the main factors hindering industrial development in South Africa, including the two structural problems named in the syllabus.
questions.expected_answer: Energy insecurity (load-shedding), deteriorating rail and port infrastructure, skills shortages and emigration, strained labour relations and strikes, crime and corruption, cheap import competition, and distance from world markets. The two structural problems: over-concentration — industry crowded into four core regions, causing congestion, high land prices and pollution there while other regions lack investment — and industrial pollution itself, e.g. the Vaal Triangle's air and Durban South's refineries, with carbon intensity increasingly taxed by trading partners.
